title: Guillain-Barre syndrome presenting with sensory disturbance following a herpes virus infection: a case report
case_prompt:
A 39-year-old man presented with sudden loss of hot and cold sensation during a shower, followed by progressive instability and weakness of his lower extremities. He also noted diplopia, dim vision, and circumoral numbness. He had had an upper respiratory infection treated with a macrolide antibiotic several days earlier. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable. He smoked 20 cigarettes daily and drank alcohol only socially. 

On examination, he had sensory loss to temperature below the T4 level, symmetric lower-limb muscle weakness, diminished patellar and ankle reflexes, blurred vision, and loss of taste. Brain MRI was normal. He was unable to stand or walk.

Two lumbar punctures—on admission and 14 days after symptom onset—showed a rise in CSF protein from 0.30 to 1.0 g/dL with normal to mildly elevated cell counts (5 to 20 cells/mm3) and negative Gram stain, cultures, and CMV PCR. 

Serologic testing revealed positive IgM antibodies for CMV, HSV, and EBV; negative results for hepatitis, HIV, VZV, and West Nile virus; and sterile blood, urine, and CSF cultures. A tuberculin skin test and CSF culture for tuberculosis were negative.

Chest X-ray and brain CT were normal; sinus imaging showed mild ethmoid and mastoid inflammation. Spinal imaging showed only degenerative changes. Electromyography revealed mildly diminished muscle activity; facial nerve stimulation failed to elicit R1 responses and showed delayed R2 responses. Motor-nerve conduction studies demonstrated absent F waves in multiple nerves, consistent with a mixed demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Guillain–Barré syndrome was diagnosed because “our patient showed progressive weakness of his lower limbs due to neuropathy, areflexia, sensory involvement and cerebella ataxia, and with the duration of the disease being less than four weeks, the required and some of the supportive diagnostic criteria for GBS were met.”  
2. HIV infection was excluded as “HIV test results were negative.”  
3. Cytomegalovirus infection was considered but excluded by virologic testing: “Blood CMV antigen and PCR tests for CMV were negative, as was the PCR test for CMV from the cerebrospinal fluid.”  
4. West Nile virus infection was ruled out because “results for West Nile virus (WNV) with indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) immunoglobulin G (IgG) and M antibody capture (MAC)-ELISA (IgM) were negative.”  
5. Varicella zoster virus infection was excluded as “varicella zoster virus (VZV) test results were negative.”  
6. Tuberculosis was excluded since “a tuberculin skin test and CSF culture for tuberculosis (TBC) were negative.”  
7. Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating syndromes, metabolic and toxic neuropathies were ruled out because “Other causes, such as multiple sclerosis (MS) or other demyelinating syndromes, diabetes mellitus, B12 vitamin deficiency, drugs and chemical neuropathies were excluded following historical, clinical, laboratory and imaging tests.”  
8. Vasculitic, autoimmune, and paraneoplastic neuropathies were excluded as “examination for vasculitides, Sjögren's syndrome, sarcoidosis and paraneoplastic neuropathy proved negative.”
